planting.note: Fast-maturing miniature onion; can also be direct-sown for baby bunching onions once soil is workable.

directions: This Dutch heirloom produces round, golf-ball-sized bulbs with glossy burgundy skin that fades to a soft pastel pink once cooked or pickled. Because it matures far faster than standard storage onions, it can be harvested young as a purple-tipped bunching onion or left to size up into a small mild bulb. The flavor is notably gentle, making raw slices in salads or quick pickles a popular use. Cluster plantings closely since bulbs stay small even at maturity, and harvest as soon as tops begin to fall for the sweetest flavor.

planting.note: Intermediate-to-long-day heirloom; needs roughly 12-16 hours of daylight to bulb properly.

directions: A centuries-old open-pollinated onion from the countryside around Milan, prized for its teardrop-shaped bulbs with deep garnet skin and pink-streaked white flesh. Give plants rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through bulb swell, then withhold water once tops begin to yellow and topple. Cure bulbs in a warm, airy location for two to three weeks before storage; this variety is noted for holding firm and flavorful well into winter. The rich, slightly sharp flavor mellows nicely when roasted or grilled.

common_name: Redwing Onion (F1 Hybrid Long-Storage Red Onion)

planting.note: Intermediate-day F1 hybrid; late-maturing, so transplants outperform direct seeding in most climates.

directions: Bred for the market grower who needs a red onion that actually lasts through winter, Redwing forms uniform, hard globes with thick, deep-red skins that resist bruising in storage. Start seed indoors under lights and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed, spacing plants to encourage full-sized bulbs. Its late maturity means it needs a full season, but the payoff is a storage onion whose color and firmness actually improve over months in a cool, dry room. Reduce watering as tops begin to fall and cure thoroughly before bagging for storage.

common_name: Highlander Onion (F1 Hybrid Early Yellow Onion)

planting.note: Extra-early long-day hybrid; can be direct-seeded as soon as soil can be worked.

directions: This extra-early long-day hybrid delivers large, uniform globes with light brown skin well before most main-season yellow onions are ready, making it a favorite for growers who want an early fresh-market crop. Direct-seed into fertile, well-worked soil as early as the ground can be tilled, thinning to final spacing once seedlings are a few inches tall. Because it bulbs quickly rather than storing long-term, plan to use or sell the crop within a few months of harvest rather than holding it over winter. Keep beds weed-free and evenly moist through bulb formation for the largest, most uniform onions.

common_name: Autumn Mammoth Leek (Giant of Elbeuf Heirloom)

planting.note: Long-season autumn leek; start early indoors for shanks to reach full mammoth size before fall harvest.

directions: Also known historically as the Giant of Elbeuf, this Normandy heirloom is grown for its exceptionally thick, short shanks rather than height, with broad light-green fans of foliage instead of the blue-tinted leaves typical of winter types. Start seed early indoors since this is one of the longest-season leeks available, then transplant into deep holes or trenches and hill soil progressively around the stems as they thicken to maximize blanched length. It tolerates hard frost and can remain in the ground into early winter without losing quality. The mild, completely fiber-free white flesh is especially prized for braising and gratins.

planting.note: Plant cloves in fall; Creole types need less cold vernalization than northern hardnecks, making them reliable in mild-winter climates.

directions: Brought to the United States from Spain by way of Nevada growers in the early 1990s, Ajo Rojo is a Creole-type softneck prized for its brilliant purple-streaked clove wrappers and adaptability to hot, arid regions where hardneck garlics struggle. Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up in fall in well-drained soil, mulching lightly over winter in colder zones. The flavor is mild and creamy when roasted but builds into a slow, powerful heat when eaten raw, making it popular with cooks who want garlic with real punch. Harvest when the lower third of leaves has browned, then cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks; Creole types store notably longer than most hardnecks.

planting.note: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in fall; Artichoke types adapt well from cold to mild-winter zones.

directions: Collected near Tochliavri in the Republic of Georgia in the late 1980s, Red Toch is an Artichoke-type softneck valued among garlic growers for the striking red and pink streaking on its clove wrappers. Plant cloves pointed-end-up in fertile, well-drained soil in fall and mulch to protect against winter heaving. It forms the overlapping, many-layered cloves typical of Artichoke garlics, with a flavor that is well balanced rather than sharply hot, making it popular both raw and cooked. Harvest once the lower leaves have dried while four or five green leaves remain, then cure for three to four weeks before storing.
